title: About
description: Jack Rome works on the bridge between people and the systems they're expected to use. Enterprise accounts at Fuel Cycle, freelance since 2016, and a Master Certified Life Coach.
keywords: biography bio background experience who Jack Rome Maryland
text: About I've spent my career on the bridge between people and the systems they're expected to use. At Fuel Cycle I manage enterprise accounts for an AI-powered market research platform. I spend most of my day translating between clients and the people who built the product. I also build internal tools and workflows for my own team, which is where most of my AI work started. I've been freelancing since 2016 and never stopped: websites, events, video editing, podcast production, graphic design, and pretty much any digital work that's helpful. Nearly all of it referred, and much of it for nonprofits and small teams working past their capacity. I also support web events for the Foundation for Inner Peace , the publisher of A Course in Miracles . Let's chat What I care about most New digital tools, especially AI tools, keep getting easier to pick up. I fully expect that to continue exponentially. But what hasn't gotten easier is everything after that: knowing what to ask for, where it fits in the work you already do, and when to trust what comes back. Most people I work with are stuck a step before all of that, and from down there, it can look like an impassable mountain. Most of my work is being the person on the mountain slope with a hand down, showing you where to put your foot as you climb. I'm proficient with the technical things, but I'm not in a rush and don't need you to already understand anything. Ideally, you should leave our work together more capable than when you started, and perhaps eventually, you won't need me anymore. A bit more about me I am a Master Certified Life Coach, trained under the ICF coaching model , make music as Jackintheway , create videos on YouTube , and speak at events . None of that is a hobby I keep separate from my work. In fact, the reason I can explain technical things to the non-technical person is that I've spent most of my life doing non-technical communication, where the work is about meeting someone exactly where they are. text: AI Enablement You don't need to be technical to use AI well. AI training, workflow design, and systems for nonprofits, small teams, and individuals, built around the people who have to use it. Book a call Email me What this looks like Three options, depending on what you need. Teaching A live session where I show your team what these tools do, what they don't, and where the risks are. People leave knowing how to use it properly. Building I make tools that run in your browser. A searchable reference or a calculator can be a standalone file, with no login. A drafting assistant or research tool that calls an AI model needs a service behind it. We agree on accounts, data access, and any running costs before I build. Untangling For teams and individuals who have already started, but it isn't working. I find where the workflow breaks, fix that part, and optimize the setup. What it's for Most teams I meet are doing the work of ten people with five, and hiring their way out isn't in the budget. Hours saved only matter because of what you spend them on instead: the relationships, the mission, and the work only your people can do. How I work My focus is enablement. I teach toward the day you don't need me, the same as I have for ten years of freelance work, nearly all of it referred. Expect documentation you own, prompts you can edit, and an honest answer when the thing you're asking for isn't worth building. See case studies Explore AI Portfolio A client asked me a simple question about her website. Would her writing be used to train AI? The short, specific answer was no, but the true, accurate answer took a few minutes and came with several conditions. I gave her the accurate one. What I won't do I won't help you replace people with software. My north star is human-centered AI enablement. I won't put your data somewhere you don't understand. Everything I build has a human approval step if you want it. I won't tell you to use AI when it's unnecessary or inappropriate for the project. That comes up fairly often. Not sure where to start? Let's chat. We'll have 45 minutes to talk about what you're trying to do, where you're getting stuck, and whether I can help. You can bring a question or show me what you're working on. title: AI Portfolio
description: Tools I’ve built for my own work, and projects I’ve worked through with clients using Claude Code and Codex.
keywords: AI tools skills Claude Code Codex agents personal knowledge systems Obsidian portfolio
text: AI Portfolio How I work with AI. Tools I’ve built for my own work, and projects I’ve worked through with clients using Claude Code and Codex. Book a call See case studies As AI tools advance, the question of using these tools is much less about technical ability and much more about willingness. But most people I talk to that want to work with AI have the same worry about it. They're afraid of finding out afterward that something went out in their name that they never approved of, or wouldn't have been comfortable putting in front of other people. The boundaries are curated to the task. Tools that read my notes can report what they find without changing the source. New material for my Obsidian vault goes into a folder called Compost, which I review myself. A save point changes Git history; a handoff can be a note in chat or an update to a project's existing handoff file. Each tool spells out where it can write and which actions need my approval. See /handoff at work This website has a shared handoff that Claude Code and Codex can both read. Here's a recorded example from an update to its links, shortened for this walkthrough. My request, excerpt Make the links arrive somewhere specific. Spoken aloud using Wispr Flow. One example: the Wayspace album in Music should link to its lyrics in Writing. See where that link goes now Before writing the note Check what changed and what was decided. js/wayspace.js The 16 cross-room links have specific destinations. Album membership comes from the catalogue. wayspace/writing.html & css/wayspace.css Writing has album filters. Linked entries have room to clear the navigation at the top. CLAUDE.md & HANDOFF.md The shared instructions keep our decisions separate from the current checkpoint. Saved version & browser checks Save point 633121a records the update. All 16 links were followed locally, and Writing showed 6 Feivel Speaks lyrics and 12 Wayspace lyrics. September 12, 2026 checkpoint A note the next session can pick up. A shortened version of the project's handoff at that point. This records the local review stage of the update. What we're doing Finish the approved website audit changes and make the cross-room links precise. Verified at this checkpoint The link update is saved as 633121a. All 16 cross-room links reach their intended destinations in the local preview. Writing's album filters show 6 Feivel Speaks lyrics and 12 Wayspace lyrics. Settled with Jack Keep the existing public Production credits for credibility. Use explicit catalogue membership for the lyric filters. Publication needs Jack's go. Still open Jack is reviewing the case study and revised copy. Nothing from this update has been pushed or deployed. Hosting-specific checks need a deployment first. Next action Review the local changes with Jack before publishing. What travels with it CLAUDE.md, HANDOFF.md, js/wayspace.js, wayspace/writing.html, css/wayspace.css, and save point 633121a. Recheck the current files and Git state when you resume. What they refuse to do Almost every one of these tools has a section in it titled "What this skill is not." These are lines from those sections, as written. Findings are observations, not action items. A tool that walks through my notes reports what it sees and stops there. It doesn't hand me a task list I didn't ask for. Never a guilt engine. One of these finds the parts of my archive I've stopped visiting. If a finding would land as "you neglected this," it gets reframed or dropped. No hooks, no scheduled runs, no committing behind my back. The tool that version-controls my writing never runs on its own. Every save point is taken on purpose. It never invents something the material didn't ask for. The tool that proposes new notes can only propose what the sources already pointed at twice. It never creates missing files, edits links, renames anything, or updates the registry. It reads, it reports, and any repair is a separate job I have to authorize. The raw text is preserved exactly. Nothing is rewritten, summarized, or cleaned up. The annotation tool adds structure around my words and never touches the words. A few of the skills /map-maker When you have piles of material, whether files, pages, transcripts, a folder nobody has opened in a year, map-maker reads all of it and gives you one place to read it from, in whatever format you want: a web page, a Word doc, a PDF, a deck. Every statement on the map carries a coordinate back to where it came from, precise enough to act on: a filename and a heading, a page number, a timestamp. So you read the consolidated view, hit something you want to be sure about, and go straight to the exact spot in the source. Where a line pulls a few sources together and doesn't have one origin, it says so, so you can always tell what came from your material and what got added to connect it. /handoff A long piece of work usually doesn't finish in one sitting. Handoff writes the note that lets the next session pick up without losing what this one learned: what got decided, what got ruled out and why, what's still open, and the one next thing to do. That can be a note I carry into another chat or a shared file that Claude Code and Codex both read. I use both, so the context needs to travel between them. It checks its own claims against the files before it writes them down, because notes like this go stale and nobody notices until they've already acted on one. It also marks which lines are verified and which are just the last session's read, so an assumption can't get laundered into a fact three sessions later. /ingest-transcript Anyone publishing long recorded conversations runs into the same thing, which is that somebody has to get through a two hour transcript and decide what to cut before it ships. This reads the whole thing and hands back one timestamped report covering what has to come out because a speaker asked for it on the record, what's worth listening to again before deciding, the standout lines worth pulling as clips, and any passage where someone recited from a published text long enough to earn a quote card on screen. It asks one question before it starts, which is what comes before this transcript in the finished file and how long that runs. Every time it reports is offset to match the editor's timeline instead of the transcript's. Without that, somebody does the arithmetic by hand for every entry, which is worse than getting no timestamps at all. /save-points I'm not a professional developer, and version control is one of the most useful things I've picked up. Most people never get near it, because the tooling assumes you already speak the language. This skill makes the process simple and easy to understand, and the skill ensures that the save points resemble save states of a video game. It tells me what changed since last time in ordinary words, proposes a description, and commits when I say yes. Anything that could lose work gets explained in full before it runs, and it teaches me one small thing per session when there's a natural opening. Some more skills /sweep walks a section of the archive and reports what it notices, with an explicit guard against drifting from noticing into telling me what to build. /portal surfaces what I've stopped paying attention to, written so that going quiet is never framed as a failure. /mycelium reads the wikilinks running through my notes: the connective tissue I use in Obsidian for writing, journaling, documentation, lyrics, and drawing themes and parallels across years of material. It never fixes a link itself, and it weighs the ones I made by hand more heavily than the ones an assistant added, so an assistant's habits can't masquerade as my own intent. /orient finds where my written instructions have drifted from reality, and revises only the lines that actually drifted. Every sentence still true stays untouched, word for word. /harvest gathers ideas flagged across months of work and ranks them by how often the material asked, rather than by how good they sound. /deliver runs with a confirmation at every stage, which flags a file that looks miscategorized instead of silently reclassifying it, and never overwrites anything. /obsidian-layer adds structure and cross-references to raw text without altering a word of it. /conversation-archiver records both halves of a dialogue with an AI, and cross-references only my words, so the record has both of us in it and the connections through it are mine. /synthesis returns what's useful, what doesn't fit, and where the source and I actually disagree, on the theory that friction is more useful than agreement. The verification tool holds the checks that catch what a browser hides: a stylesheet returning the wrong content type, an import that 404s without breaking the page, a phone-width test that was never actually testing a phone. This one came out of me pointing Claude Code at the last couple of months of my project history and asking what was worth building, based on the repetitive work we were doing. How this works with clients The tools above support my own work. These case studies follow projects I worked through with clients: what we needed, what we tried, what changed, and how we checked it. What carries over Regardless of the tool, room, or industry, these practices support my workflows across the board. The onboarding ships inside the tool. An intake interview on the first run, and something behind it anyone can ask a question of at any point. A new person can start without a walkthrough and stay unstuck without booking time with me. It handles the part where a tool gets shipped to a team and then nobody uses it. The context lives in plain files you own. It stays in plain markdown rather than locked inside one platform's project or one person's account, so it follows whoever needs it and survives a change of model, of tool, or of employer. Anything irreversible waits for a person. The approval steps depend on the task and the permission already given. A report can go into an agreed folder; sending it to someone or changing the source calls for its own permission. The prompt carries the context, so you don't have to write one. The domain knowledge, the format rules, and the voice go into the tool. What comes back is ready to send rather than ready to rewrite, and nobody has to learn prompting first. Reference that people actually open. Scattered documents become one page with search and filters, so the answer is findable in the moment someone needs it. It replaces the folder nobody opens with a page people keep in a tab. The value of curation Knowing exactly who a tool is for, and what they need to use a tool on their own, is most of what makes enablement work. When we build empathically, the tools become too convenient not to use, because we took the time to understand each use case carefully. Tools that a team can use, or anyone who comes across them, are absolutely worth building, but they don't have to be generic. These tools work best when they keep their tailored DNA as placeholders, ready to adapt to the next person during an introductory onboarding step at first use. Mine started with one person, which is me, and that's an honest place for curation to start. Want something like this for your team? How I work → Book a call

title: Remastering an event with Codex
description: Two installments of a recorded-event remaster: editable graphics, timing maps, and checks that had to preserve the editor's deliberate exceptions.
keywords: Codex remaster event editing automation After Effects editable graphics card Spanish translation audio case study
text: ← AI Portfolio · Case study Remastering an event with Codex. I worked with Codex on graphics and timeline automation for two installments of a recorded event. The workflow had to keep up with changes I was making by hand. Part 1: keeping the timing traceable The first installment began with information cards. I had the copy in a spreadsheet and an existing animation to work from. The job grew to include still images, removals, and audio repairs. There was also a Spanish recording made against the earlier English version. Every change to the edit could affect where that translation belonged. I had mostly deleted things and left gaps, but there were a few moments where I had to shift things, and some ended up extending a bit. Keeping the gaps was no longer enough to preserve the original timing. Three timelines to keep track of The same material, at different times 1. Original recording The Spanish recording followed this version. A × B ‖ C 2. Revised edit with gaps An extension moves later material. A removal leaves empty time. A + × B ‖ C 3. Final edit Close the selected removal gap. Keep the extension and the pause. A + B ‖ C A B C Retained passages + Editorial extension × Selected removal ‖ Intentional pause Conceptual example, not the event's timeline or scale. In the saved production pass, 4 selected closures removed 2,464 frames: 98.56 seconds at 25 fps. We needed to map where each retained passage came from and where it ended up. The version labeled "with gaps" already included my extensions, so its name couldn't tell us which clock we were looking at. Some empty stretches were there because I wanted a pause. I wanted a little breather at the end, for example. Those needed to stay when we closed the gaps left by removed material. A map between the versions Codex turned the editing notes into a cue sheet, with timing recorded in integer frames at the sequence's verified 25 fps. I reviewed the planned actions before each editing pass, and the saved project was checked afterward. The initial pass placed 48 visual inserts: 19 information cards and 29 still images. Removals first left gaps. Once I had finished my refinements, 4 selected gaps were closed from the end backward, with the other sequences protected. For the Spanish audio, the map selected 7 retained source segments and placed them in the final edit, with 6 intentional silent intervals. Each segment kept its playback speed. The original recording stayed on a muted track, and the conformed audio went on a separate track for review. We also made a bilingual timing-review document to help locate passages. Its speech-recognition text could guide listening, but still needed checking against the audio. What needed another pass Moving the clips hadn't settled the transitions. Their positions were stored separately and needed a correction pass. We also had to refresh the English transcript after the final timing changes. The first graphics delivery contained rendered cards and structured copy data, but the promised editable After Effects builder was missing. That became one of the jobs for the second installment. Part 2: rebuilding the editable system The next installment needed 35 information cards and 39 supplied still images. I was still reframing photos and adjusting transitions while the automation work was underway, so each pass needed to start from the current saved edit. We rebuilt the graphics system from the approved renders and previews. I approved 3 prototypes before the batch: a long card, a biography, and a short card. Their sampled transparency bounds matched the references, with text-line endpoints no more than 2 pixels apart. This time, the delivery included the editable After Effects project, the builder, and structured text data, alongside 35 transparent renders and 35 previews. New types of layout would still need their own prototype review. I set the treatment for the photos by hand. Codex continued that pattern for the remaining stills: replace the picture, keep the program audio, and use the demonstrated 30-frame transitions. A video contribution inside a nested sequence also needed repair. Two broad attempts failed their checks and stopped without saving. A narrower repair fixed the picture join and restored the known transitions, then checked the saved result. The two cards I had moved The final audit reset all 35 cards to the default framing. I had deliberately moved 2 of them because faces were low in the frame. Making those cards match the others undid an editing decision. After I pointed it out, their exact approved offsets were restored and checked in the saved project. The check needed to account for those exceptions, and the rule it had been using didn't. 35 cards, with 2 deliberate exceptions Check the approved framing for each card 33 Default framing Keep the shared scale and position. 2 Approved exceptions Keep the offsets I chose to leave faces visible. Schematic of the corrected framing. The 2 positions were restored after the audit had reset them. A reusable exception registry is a proposed next step. What each installment produced Part 1 20 rendered information cards, including a later short card. The initial automated pass placed 19 cards and 29 stills. The Spanish audio file matched its planned sample count, with zero-valued samples in all 6 intended silence windows. The saved listening checklist and 20 translated-card reviews were still open. Part 2 An editable graphics system with 35 renders and previews. All 39 stills were integrated through my manual work and the automated continuation. Final verification matched 10 protected sequences to their reference snapshots. I exported the locked English master and reported that it was broadcast. The export's metadata and stream analysis matched the technical delivery format and reported no errors. This account draws on the two exhibit packages and their saved reports and artifact checks. It does not add an independent full-playback review of either installment or independent observation of the broadcast. What still needs work Part 2's Spanish conform is still open. Part 1 produced a technically checked review file, but its saved record also stops before listening approval. The second run doesn't establish that the language workflow has been tested end to end again. The next improvement is to record approved exceptions before running a check: which card changed, the exact setting, why I changed it, and the saved version where I approved it. Once I say an edit is ready to lock, any further change needs my go. The reusable workflow documents carry those rules forward. Graphics, captions, and language review keep their own approval steps, and a changed final edit needs a new timing map. ← Back to AI Portfolio Book a call

title: Automating a two-track class edit
description: Turning a class transcript and hand-cut examples into a checked Premiere edit, including the mistakes and the limits of the checks.
keywords: Claude Code premiere transcript teaching class two track editing automation case study
text: ← AI Portfolio · Case study Automating a two-track class edit from a transcript. I worked with Claude to turn my editing decisions into a cue sheet and scripts, then checked each pass against the saved Premiere project. The edit I was editing a recorded class in Premiere Pro. The speaker and the slides were recorded on separate, synchronized video tracks, with the slides covering the speaker. I needed to choose which one appeared, then remove the discussion sections and the short requests to advance a slide. I had already cut the first 10 minutes by hand. I noticed the speaker often said "so" when he started reading a slide, and asked Claude to find those moments in the transcript. How a 92-minute recording became a teaching cut 92 minutes recorded Two presentation blocks, discussion between them, and more discussion afterward. 51:15 of class material I cut off the discussion at the end and kept the outro. The middle discussion still needed to come out. 34:13 verified teaching cut The script lifted the middle discussion and 18 short asides. I closed the verified gaps in Premiere. Slides Shown Hidden Shown Speaker Under slides Visible Under slides Track illustration, not to scale; runtimes rounded to seconds. At the verified checkpoint, the outro ended at 34:28. Two later corrections are described below. The rules came from my hand cuts Claude compared its cue sheet with the decisions already saved in my project. 19 of the 21 show/hide decisions matched. The two differences helped explain my choices: I opened on the speaker, and I kept the speaker on screen through a brief slide title instead of flashing the slide up for a few seconds. We used those cuts to guide the rest: hold a slide for at least 6 seconds and the speaker for at least 8, with a shorter allowance during a slide request. Those were starting rules for this recording. I still needed to watch the transitions. We considered exporting the sequence, changing it elsewhere, and importing it again. Reading the project exposed audio processing and proxy links that the proposed rebuild wouldn't preserve. We chose an in-place script to protect the already-finished audio work. I ran a dry run first, reviewed its report, then ran the script in a duplicate project. It cut the slide track and disabled the sections where the speaker should be visible. Reading the saved file confirmed all 61 segments in the planned region matched the cue sheet. The earlier hand cuts were unchanged. Keeping the tracks together during removal Lift the same ranges Remove material from both video tracks and both audio tracks, leaving gaps. Later clips stay at their original times. Check the saved project Compare the start and end of every gap across all four tracks. Close the gaps Once the gaps match, use Premiere's native Close Gap command and check the saved file again. The middle discussion was just over 16 minutes. Together with 18 short asides, that made 19 removal ranges, about 17 minutes in total. Keeping the gaps open until they were checked meant the original timestamps stayed useful throughout the pass. What I caught on playback Watching the cut, I heard a slide request that should have been removed. The transcript had written it as "Fine." A search for "slide" couldn't find it. We used the saved removal map to work backward from 27:36 in the edited video to the original transcript. Claude then looked for short, isolated utterances followed by a pause and a return to slide reading. That found a second request with the same mistranscription. The keyword search and the new structural check together found 20 requests in this recording. The structural check reported no false positives in this pass. That result came from one class. It still needed checking on another. I removed the two late requests by hand. The saved project confirmed their gaps matched across all four tracks. The removal map made the missed moment easier to locate; listening was what found it. What we verified After the first Close Gap, the slides and both audio tracks ended at 34:13. The speaker track included a subscribe outro and ended at 34:28. All four tracks had zero gaps, their clip edges stayed on frame boundaries, and the title card at the beginning hadn't moved. The amount of content was unchanged across that gap-close operation. It had removed the empty spaces left by the delete pass. The two late corrections were then verified as matching gaps, totaling about 7 seconds. Closing those gaps was predicted to leave teaching through about 34:06 and the outro through 34:21. The session record ends before that last gap-close was verified. What still needs checking The timing rules and the request detector came from this class. Another recording needs its own review before those rules can be trusted there. We also didn't test running the removal script twice on the same project. The dry run and the saved-file checks let us inspect each planned pass; they don't establish that repeating it is safe. I still have to watch the edit. A file can match the cue sheet exactly and contain a cut I'd want to change. ← Back to AI Portfolio Book a call

title: Design
description: How Jack Rome's Wayspace design system got here, told in order, with the show flyers and logos made along the way.
text: Wayspace Design How the design system got here, along with some flyers, covers, and logos made along the way. How this came to be This design system has been cultivated over the course of 10 or so years, but it really started showing sprouts in 2020 when I transitioned my artistic identity from Jahn Rome to Jackintheway. That’s when the Wayspace name and early color scheme arrived, and it’s been a steady refinement ever since. 2021 The tool pack Six objects, with each one representing a different quality. Building these prototypes helped me to develop the adventurous, playful, yet tangible feel that Wayspace would come to have. 2022 Wayspace, the album This is the culmination of years of design and music growth, arriving here in Wayspace. This is an arrival, a homecoming. I built out the dimension with characters, and they welcome us! 2023 The Wayspace podcast cover I brought the puzzle pieces forward, rebuilt the wordmark out of those same blocks, and flattened the ground to blue. Now This site Six colors, one outline weight, Archivo set heavy, and a lot of squares. I built it on tokens, so every color has a name and every page reads from the same file. The swatches below come straight out of it. Orange Blue Yellow Green Salmon Brown Paper Other design work Logos and show flyers, some of them from before Wayspace had a name.
